title: Find what is using disk space
summary: Locate the biggest directories and files when a disk is filling up.

steps.title: See which filesystem is full
steps.explain: Shows each mounted filesystem with its size, used and available space.
steps.output: Look at Use% and 'Mounted on'. Only investigate the filesystem near 100%; /home and / may be separate.
errors: If space looks free but writes still fail with 'No space left on device', check inodes with df -i (too many small files).

steps.title: Find the biggest directories one level down
steps.explain: du totals each subdirectory; sort -h understands K/M/G suffixes; tail keeps the largest. 2> /dev/null hides 'Permission denied' noise from directories you cannot read.
steps.output: The last line is the total of <dir> itself. Repeat with the biggest subdirectory as the new <dir> to drill down.
errors: Totals for system directories are incomplete without root because unreadable folders are skipped. That is expected; start with your home directory.

steps.title: List individual files above a size
steps.explain: -xdev stays on one filesystem (does not wander into other mounts); -size +100M means larger than 100 MiB; ls -lh prints sizes for review.
steps.output: Typical culprits: build directories (Yocto tmp/ and downloads/ can be tens of GB), VM images, core dumps, old logs, downloads.

steps.title: Decide what to remove, deliberately
steps.explain: Nothing above deleted anything. Remove only files you recognise, by exact path, preferably moving them first or using your build system's clean target (e.g. make clean after make -n clean). Never delete files under system directories to free space; use your package manager's cleanup instead (e.g. sudo apt clean on Debian/Ubuntu).

title: Read system and service logs
summary: Find error messages from services, the kernel and the last boot.

steps.title: Is it a systemd system?
steps.explain: Process 1 is the init system. If it prints systemd, journalctl is available; otherwise logs are plain files in /var/log/ or only dmesg.
steps.output: systemd, init, or busybox/sh-like names. In containers it is often your own program.

steps.title: Errors since this boot (systemd)
steps.explain: Only messages at priority err or worse since boot.
errors: 'You are currently not seeing messages from other users and the system' means you need to be in the systemd-journal or adm group (depends on distribution) or use sudo.

steps.title: One service's logs
steps.explain: The last 100 lines for a single service, such as ssh or NetworkManager. systemctl status <service> shows the same tail plus its state.

steps.title: Follow a plain log file (non-systemd)
steps.explain: Prints new lines as they arrive and survives log rotation. Common files: /var/log/syslog (Debian), /var/log/messages (RHEL, BusyBox syslogd).
errors: 'Permission denied' on /var/log files: many are readable only by root or the adm group.

steps.title: Kernel and driver messages
steps.explain: Hardware, USB and driver problems usually show up here.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to read the kernel log (needed when kernel.dmesg_restrict=1).
errors: 'dmesg: read kernel buffer failed: Operation not permitted' means dmesg_restrict is on; use sudo or journalctl -k.

title: Check which ports are listening
summary: See which programs accept network connections, and on which addresses.

steps.title: List listening TCP and UDP sockets
steps.explain: -t TCP, -u UDP, -l listening only, -n numeric ports (no name lookup).
steps.output: Local Address:Port tells you where it listens: 127.0.0.1 or [::1] = this machine only; 0.0.0.0 or [::] or * = all interfaces, reachable from the network unless a firewall blocks it.

steps.title: Show which process owns each socket
steps.explain: -p adds users:(("name",pid=...)). Without root you only see your own processes.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to see other users' process names.

steps.title: Test it from this machine
steps.explain: For HTTP services: prints response headers. 'Connection refused' means nothing listens on that address/port.

title: Find the process using a port
summary: Fix 'Address already in use' by finding which program holds the port.

steps.title: Find the listener on the port
steps.explain: The filter shows only sockets whose source port is <port>. Quoted so the shell passes it as one argument.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to read process names.
steps.output: users:(("name",pid=1234,fd=3)) gives the program and PID.

steps.title: Alternative with lsof
steps.explain: Lists open network files using that port, with COMMAND and PID columns.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to see other users' processes.

steps.title: Check what that PID is before acting
steps.explain: Shows owner, how long it has run, and the full command line. Make sure it is your leftover program, not a system service.

steps.title: Stop it politely
steps.explain: Sends SIGTERM so the program can clean up. If it is a systemd service, use sudo systemctl stop <service> instead, or it may be restarted.
steps.warning: The program stops and loses unsaved state. Double-check the PID: PIDs are reused, so do not rely on an old number.

title: Find what is slowing the machine down
summary: Identify processes using the most CPU or memory.

steps.title: Overall load and memory
steps.explain: Load average vs nproc tells you if the CPUs are overloaded; free shows memory and swap.
steps.output: Use the 'available' column, not 'free': Linux uses spare RAM as cache and gives it back when needed.

steps.title: Top processes by CPU
steps.explain: A snapshot sorted by CPU. Run top for a live view (press M to sort by memory, q to quit).

steps.title: Top processes by memory
steps.explain: RSS is resident memory in KiB.

steps.title: Did the kernel kill something for memory?
steps.explain: The OOM killer logs which process it killed.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to read the kernel log.

title: Find recently changed files
summary: See which files changed in the last minutes or days, e.g. after a build or install.

steps.title: Files modified in the last 60 minutes
steps.explain: -mmin -60 means modified less than 60 minutes ago. Use -mtime -2 for the last 2 days.

steps.title: Newest files first in one directory
steps.explain: -t sorts by modification time, newest first.

steps.title: Exact timestamps of one file
steps.explain: Modify = content changed; Change = metadata (permissions, owner) changed; Access may not update on every read (relatime).

title: Search a codebase for a function or message
summary: Find where a symbol, error message or config option is defined and used.

steps.title: Recursive search with line numbers
steps.explain: -r recurses, -n shows line numbers. Single quotes keep the shell from changing $, * or spaces in <text>; -- protects text starting with -.
steps.output: path:line:matching line. No output and exit status 1 means no match.

steps.title: Only C sources and headers, whole words
steps.explain: -w avoids matching probe inside my_probe_helper. --include limits file types.

steps.title: Inside a git repository
steps.explain: Faster, and skips untracked build output automatically.

title: Compile and run a C program
summary: From hello.c to a running program, and how to read compiler errors.

steps.title: Check the compiler is installed
steps.explain: 'command not found' means install it: build-essential (Debian/Ubuntu), gcc (Fedora), base-devel (Arch), build-base (Alpine).

steps.title: Compile with warnings and debug info
steps.explain: Creates the executable hello in the current directory.
steps.output: Silence means success. Warnings start with file:line:column: warning:, errors with error:.
errors: 'undefined reference to `foo`' is a linker error: the function's .c file or library (-l...) is missing from the command.
'fatal error: xyz.h: No such file or directory': install the library's -dev/-devel package or add -I<dir>.

steps.title: Run it
steps.explain: ./ is needed because the current directory is not on PATH (deliberately, for safety).
errors: 'Permission denied' usually means the file is not executable or lives on a filesystem mounted noexec.
'cannot execute binary file: Exec format error' means it was built for another architecture.

steps.title: Check the exit status
steps.explain: Prints the return value of main from the previous command: 0 means success.

title: Build a project with make
summary: Run an existing Makefile, understand its output, and fix common errors.

steps.title: Preview what make will do
steps.explain: Prints the commands without running them.

steps.title: Build
steps.explain: Builds in parallel using all CPU cores.
errors: '*** missing separator': a recipe line starts with spaces instead of a Tab; check with cat -A Makefile (tabs show as ^I).
'No rule to make target X': a source file named in the Makefile does not exist, or you are in the wrong directory.
If errors scroll past, rerun plain make (no -j) to see the first error in order.

steps.title: Force a rebuild
steps.explain: Rebuilds all targets even if they look up to date; useful after changing compiler flags.

title: Inspect an executable or object file
summary: Find a binary's architecture, linked libraries and symbols, e.g. before copying it to a board.

steps.title: What kind of file is it?
steps.explain: Reports ELF class (32/64-bit), architecture (x86-64, ARM aarch64, ...), dynamic or static linking, and whether it is stripped.
steps.output: Compare the architecture with uname -m on the machine where it should run.

steps.title: Header details
steps.explain: Machine and Type fields; works for any architecture.

steps.title: Needed shared libraries (safe for untrusted files)
steps.explain: Each library must exist on the target system. On the target itself, ldd shows where they resolve, but only use ldd on trusted binaries.

steps.title: Is a function defined or missing?
steps.explain: T = defined here, U = needed from a library. Stripped binaries show 'no symbols'; try nm -D.

title: Inspect, load and unload a kernel module
summary: Safe order of steps for testing your own driver module on a test machine.

steps.title: Use a VM or test board
steps.explain: Module code runs inside the kernel. A bug can freeze or crash the whole machine and lose unsaved work. Practise in a virtual machine or on a development board, not on the computer you depend on.

steps.title: Check the running kernel version
steps.explain: Your module must be built against headers for exactly this version (e.g. package linux-headers-$(uname -r) on Debian/Ubuntu).

steps.title: Check your module matches
steps.explain: Compare vermagic with uname -r; also check license and parm (parameters).

steps.title: Watch the kernel log in a second terminal
steps.explain: Your pr_info()/dev_info() messages and any oops appear here.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to read the kernel log.

steps.title: Load it
steps.explain: Runs your module_init function.
steps.warning: Runs your code in the kernel as root; bugs can crash the system. Test machine only.
errors: 'Invalid module format': vermagic mismatch, rebuild against the running kernel.
'Operation not permitted': not root, or Secure Boot/lockdown requires signed modules.
'Unknown symbol in module': see dmesg; often a missing dependency (use modprobe for installed modules) or a GPL-only symbol used by a non-GPL module.

steps.title: Confirm it is loaded
steps.explain: Shows size and how many users it has.

steps.title: Unload it
steps.explain: Runs your module_exit function; check dmesg for its messages.
steps.warning: Only unload your own test module. 'Module is in use' means a process still has its device open.

title: Check whether a USB device was detected
summary: Plug in a USB device or USB-serial adapter and confirm the kernel saw it and bound a driver.

steps.title: Watch kernel messages, then plug it in
steps.explain: Look for 'new USB device', the vendor/product IDs, and lines like 'now attached to ttyUSB0'. Ctrl+C when done.
steps.warning: sudo is used only to read the kernel log.
errors: No message at all: try another cable (many are charge-only) or port. In WSL, USB devices must first be attached with usbipd on Windows; in VMs, pass the device through.

steps.title: List USB devices
steps.explain: Each line has ID vendor:product. Note the ID to search for the right driver.

steps.title: See which driver is bound
steps.explain: Tree view with Driver=... per interface. Driver=[none] means no driver claimed it.

steps.title: Find the device node
steps.explain: USB-serial adapters usually appear as ttyUSB0 (FTDI/CP210x/CH340) or ttyACM0 (CDC-ACM, many dev boards). 'No such file or directory' for one pattern is normal.

title: Fix 'Permission denied' on a serial port
summary: Get access to /dev/ttyUSB0 without running your serial terminal as root.

steps.title: Check the device's owner group
steps.explain: <device> such as /dev/ttyUSB0.
steps.output: e.g. crw-rw---- 1 root dialout ...: owner root and group dialout can read/write; everyone else cannot. Some distributions use uucp instead of dialout.

steps.title: Check your groups
steps.explain: If that group is missing from groups=..., you are not allowed to open the port.

steps.title: Add yourself to that group
steps.explain: -a appends; without it, -G would replace all your supplementary groups.
steps.warning: Changes your account as root. Double-check -a is present and the group name is right; membership grants access to all serial devices.
errors: Membership only applies to new logins: log out and back in (or reboot), then run id again.

title: Write an image to an SD card (inspect first)
summary: Identify the right device before writing a Yocto/Raspberry Pi image; the wrong device means data loss.

steps.title: Verify the image
steps.explain: Compare with the published checksum before writing.

steps.title: List disks BEFORE inserting the card
steps.explain: Remember what you see. Then insert the card and run it again: the new disk (e.g. sdb or mmcblk0) is the card. Check its size matches.
errors: Older util-linux uses MOUNTPOINT (singular) instead of MOUNTPOINTS.

steps.title: Unmount any auto-mounted partitions of the card
steps.explain: Repeat for each mounted partition of the card only (e.g. /dev/sdb1).
steps.warning: Make sure the partition belongs to the card, not your system disk.

steps.title: Write the image
steps.cmd: sudo dd if=<image> of=<card-device> bs=4M conv=fsync status=progress
steps.explain: <card-device> is the whole disk (e.g. /dev/sdX or /dev/mmcblk0), not a partition. Many projects recommend bmaptool for .wic images; it is faster and verifies.
steps.warning: dd overwrites the target device completely without asking. Choosing your system disk destroys your operating system and files. Re-check lsblk immediately before running.
errors: 'Permission denied' means you forgot sudo; 'No space left on device' at the very end can happen when the image is larger than the card.

steps.title: Flush and eject
steps.explain: Waits until all cached writes reach the card before you remove it.

title: Archive a directory and copy it elsewhere
summary: Pack a project into a tarball, verify it, and copy it to another machine.

steps.title: Create the archive
steps.explain: Run from the parent of <dir> so paths in the archive start with <dir>/.
steps.warning: Overwrites an existing <name>.tar.gz.

steps.title: Check what is inside
steps.explain: Confirms the files and paths look right.

steps.title: Copy to another machine
steps.explain: For repeated syncing of a whole directory, rsync -av --dry-run first, then without --dry-run.
steps.warning: Overwrites a file with the same name on the remote side.

title: Fix 'Permission denied' when running a script
summary: Understand execute permission, the shebang line and noexec mounts.

steps.title: Look at the permissions
steps.explain: -rw-r--r-- has no x: it is not executable.

steps.title: Make it executable for you
steps.explain: Adds execute for the owner only. Avoid chmod 777: it lets every user modify the file.

steps.title: Check the first line
steps.explain: Should be a shebang such as #!/bin/sh or #!/usr/bin/env bash.
errors: 'bad interpreter: No such file or directory': the interpreter path is wrong, or the file has Windows line endings (shown as /bin/sh^M); convert with sed -i 's/\r$//' <script> or dos2unix.

steps.title: Still denied? Check the filesystem
steps.explain: If OPTIONS contains noexec (common for /tmp, USB sticks, some Windows mounts), run it as sh <script> or copy it elsewhere.

title: Redirection: overwrite (>) vs append (>>), and stderr
summary: Send output to files without accidentally wiping them.

steps.title: > replaces the whole file
steps.explain: The shell empties <file> before the command even starts. If <file> held important data, it is gone.
steps.warning: Overwrites <file> without asking. In bash, set -o noclobber makes > refuse to overwrite existing files.

steps.title: >> appends to the end
steps.explain: Creates the file if missing, otherwise adds a line at the end.

steps.title: Errors go to a separate stream
steps.explain: 1 (stdout) is normal output, 2 (stderr) is error messages. Each can be redirected separately.
steps.warning: Overwrites out.txt and err.txt in the current directory.

steps.title: Both streams into one file
steps.explain: Order matters: first point stdout at the file, then 2>&1 makes stderr go where stdout goes now. Writing 2>&1 > file sends errors to the terminal instead.
steps.warning: Overwrites build.log; use >> to keep previous logs.

steps.title: Discard noise
steps.explain: /dev/null throws away whatever is written to it, here the 'Permission denied' messages.

steps.title: Writing to root-owned files
steps.explain: sudo echo ... > file fails because the redirection is done by your own shell, not by sudo. tee runs as root and -a appends.
steps.warning: Writes to a system file as root. Without -a, tee overwrites the file. Back up the file first.

title: Quoting, spaces and special characters
summary: Why file names with spaces break commands, and when to use '...' vs "...".

steps.title: Spaces split words
steps.explain: Without quotes the shell passes three separate names: file, with, spaces.txt.

steps.title: Single quotes: everything literal
steps.explain: Nothing is expanded inside single quotes: no $variables, no * globs.

steps.title: Double quotes: variables expand, but stay one word
steps.explain: Always write "$var" when using variables that contain paths, so spaces do not split them.

steps.title: Placeholders on this site
steps.explain: Text like <file> is a placeholder: replace the whole thing including < and >. If your value contains spaces or special characters, wrap it in single quotes. Never leave < or > in the command: the shell treats them as redirection and may overwrite a file.

title: Pipes, exit status and chaining
summary: Connect commands with |, and use && / || and $? to react to success or failure.

steps.title: A pipe feeds one command's output into the next
steps.cmd: grep -c error <file> ; sort <file> | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
steps.explain: Each | connects stdout to the next command's stdin. Only stdout is piped; stderr still goes to the terminal.

steps.title: Exit status of the last command
steps.explain: 0 means success (grep: found). Non-zero means failure or 'not found' (grep: 1 = no match, 2 = error).

steps.title: Run the next command only if the first succeeded
steps.explain: && stops if make fails, so you never run an old binary by mistake. || runs the right side only on failure.

steps.title: Pipelines hide earlier failures
steps.explain: By default a pipeline's status is that of its last command. In bash scripts, pipefail makes the pipeline fail if any part fails. It is not available in every POSIX sh.

title: The -- option terminator
summary: Safely handle file names that start with a dash.

steps.title: Names starting with - look like options
steps.explain: Everything after -- is treated as a name, even -rf or --help. Most GNU and BusyBox tools support it.

steps.title: Searching for text that starts with a dash
steps.explain: Without --, grep would try to interpret -Wall as options.

steps.title: Alternative: prefix with ./
steps.explain: ./-name is clearly a path, so no tool mistakes it for an option.

title: sudo, root and permissions
summary: When you really need sudo, and why not to prefix everything with it.

steps.title: First ask why it was denied
steps.explain: Owner, group and rwx bits explain most 'Permission denied' errors. Often the fix is to work in your home directory or join a group (e.g. dialout), not sudo.

steps.title: Check what you may run with sudo
steps.explain: Lists the commands your account is allowed to run as root.
steps.warning: Asks for your password; it only lists rules.

steps.title: Rules of thumb
steps.explain: Use sudo only for the single command that needs it (installing packages, loading modules, writing system files). Do not build or compile with sudo: it leaves root-owned files in your project. Never run downloaded scripts with sudo before reading them. A warning label on this site does not make a command safe; you are responsible for checking targets.

title: GNU vs BusyBox, bash vs sh, systemd or not
summary: Why a command works on your PC but not on an embedded board or container.

steps.title: Which implementation is this?
steps.explain: GNU coreutils prints 'ls (GNU coreutils) ...'. BusyBox prints its own banner or an error. Many embedded images (Yocto core-image-minimal, Buildroot, Alpine) use BusyBox, which supports fewer options.

steps.title: Which shell am I using?
steps.explain: bash, dash, ash (BusyBox) or zsh. Scripts starting with #!/bin/sh should avoid bash-only features like [[ ]], arrays and pipefail; on Debian/Ubuntu /bin/sh is dash.

steps.title: Is a command a builtin, alias or program?
steps.explain: Builtins (cd, echo, export) differ between shells; programs come from packages and may be missing.

steps.title: systemd is not universal
steps.explain: systemctl and journalctl only work when systemd is the init system (check ps -p 1 -o comm=). Alpine uses OpenRC (rc-service), many BusyBox systems use /etc/init.d scripts and syslogd, and most containers run no init at all.
